utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. While entering the courtroom I was told by the Registrar that today we mark the 400th trial day. Yes, Ms. Gustafson, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. And good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And good morning, Dr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If I could have P3129, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Dr. Lukic, in your statement you talked about the issue of refugees and the return of refugees and at paragraph 33 you said that the government tried to help and look after both Serbian and Muslim refugees and did not discriminate in this respect. And at paragraph 46 you stated that the government sought the return of refugees regardless of ethnicity. Now, if we could go to page 8 of the English and page 12 of the B/C/S, and these are the government minutes from the 20th of March, 1993. And item 22, which is at the top of the B/C/S and the middle of the English, in the second-last paragraph it states: "The government emphasised the need for a synchronised and organised action to populate the free areas in the territory of Republika Srpska. To that end, conditions should be created for the return of refugees ..." And it's with respect to this particular item that you said that the government tried to help and after both Serbian and Muslim refugees. So although this document doesn't say anything about ethnicity, it's clearly your evidence that this was a non-discriminatory policy. But in fact, Dr. Lukic, your government sought to strategically populate the Republika Srpska with ethnic Serb refugees in order to create a new demographic reality in the Republika Srpska. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to draw such a conclusion, not only from this session but also from previous sessions, and first and foremost from what was going on in the field. It is correct that we had refugees from all over Bosnia and Herzegovina. I would say that a lot of them came even from Croatia, maybe half of Croatia even. What I have to say here is this: At one point in Banja Luka I felt that there were more refugees than the citizens of Banja Luka themselves. If I tell you that towards the end of the war when I returned from the university, my wife told me that an armed soldier and his wife had arrived and wanted to throw her out of our own apartment. I believe that I've already told you that --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you, but we're moving away from my question and you're getting into numbers and problems. And my question was specifically related to ethnicity. So I'd like to now go to P1379, which is the transcript of the 34th Republika Srpska Assembly Session. This is a document we looked at yesterday. We looked at a speech you made at this session, but I'd like to look at another portion of it now. And if we could go to page 212 in the English and 230 in the B/C/S. And this is a portion of the Assembly where a number of government ministers present reports on the activities of their ministries. And here we have Mr. Velibor Ostojic speaking, who was at the time a minister without portfolio in your government. And about three lines down and this is the middle in the B/C/S, at the bottom of the page in the English, he says that: "... I was leading the committee as a minister without portfolio. We were aiming to achieve our goal, which was ethnical - geographical continuity of Serb population, while accommodating the refugees, and actually we were building new demographic politics for the RS ..." And then if we go to the next page in the English, he goes on a few lines down to talk about this geographical continuity being accomplished in several priority areas, including Stara Herzegovina, Birac, and Posavina. Now, as Mr. Ostojic stated here, Dr. Lukic, the government's policy on refugees was linked with its goal of achieving the ethnical-geographical continuity of Serb population in the RS; right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, Madam Prosecutor, you interrupted me. Second of all, there was a huge problem of refugees and you simplified it. And now you are trying to take things out of the context of some discussions that don't necessarily have to be correct. I'm trying to say that we had to accommodate thousands upon thousands of people. We had to split families and we did that, and not only with our own ethnicity. We asked from other ethnicities to accommodate people. It is a well-known fact that when you talked about certain areas, that Croats lived there. They had left to Croatia and they were settled in what were formerly Serbian houses in Banija, Lika, Kordun, and Slavonia. What could we do? Are you suggesting that we should have thrown them into the river or should we have put them up in their houses? I'm not doubting that there were some other ideas on the part of some government members; however, I can only speak about the conclusions of the government and what the government supported and what I myself supported. And we also enjoyed support by Mr. Karadzic for all that. At all costs, we struggled to accommodate refugees, to protect them. And then when finally peace came of course we had to return people their property. It was only logical. And Republika Srpska was the first one that did that once the war was over.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. You said that things are being taken out of context. Let's look at what Mr. Ostojic said six months later at another Assembly session. That's P1388. And this is in March 1994, still while he was a minister in your government. And if we could go to page 168 in the English and 135 in the B/C/S. And again, Mr. Lukic, you attended this session and, in fact, you discuss your attendance at this session in paragraph 80 of your statement. And again Mr. Ostojic begins his speech while bringing up the issue of refugees. And right at the bottom of the page in the B/C/S, if we could make that a little larger, just before the number 33 in the English he says: "But the first part of the work has been done. The document that is called the Project on Demographic Policy of Republika Srpska was made. We have to deal with this problem first, in order to establish the geographic continuity of the Serbian population in RS area." And if we turn the page in the B/C/S he states that: "There are four areas that are extremely sensitive and which should be worked on. The first is old Herzegovina ... Srbinje, Visegrad, Rogatica. The second one is Birac - in the area of Vlasenica, Bratunac, Zvornik. The third one is Posavina in two directions - along the Sava ... and the outskirts of Trebova and Vlasic. The fourth one is Sana - Una area, and the fifth one Vrbas area. The Sana - Una area is Krupa, Novi, Prijedor, Kljuc, Sanski Most ..." And he says: "We lack the population ..." Now, again, Dr. Lukic, you were talking about the republic being overwhelmed with refugees, but here Mr. Ostojic is saying again that the priority is to establish the geographic continuity of the Serb population in certain areas of strategic importance where there is insufficient population. This is about populating the areas of Republika Srpska that have been emptied of Muslims and Croats with ethnic Serbs, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, for the following reason: You do not see that we in Sarajevo had 155.000 Serbs, and then towards the end of 1992 when I left only some 20- to 25.000 were still there. In Bihac we had over 40 per cent of the Serb residents and then not a single Serb remained living in Bihac. In Mostar almost all the Serbs were expelled if not killed. Let me not even talk about Zenica, Rogatica, and many other municipalities that you yourself have mentioned, and obviously those people had to be accommodated somewhere. Please, Mr. Ostojic is the last person who can interpret the government's decision. It is not my call to talk about deceased people and I'm sure that Mr. Karadzic will agree. He was not the main person there. There were four other university professors there. There were two doctors, two professors, and so on and so forth. I still claim that it was a very competent government which had to listen to all sorts of discussions, but it was not prepared to implement any of those words. And that is a fact. Please, give me just one area where we implemented such policies. The contrary was true. We asked the people to return. We wanted their property to be safe and secure. That was the principal demand. I'm sure that there were individuals who did what they did, and you know it only too well. We don't even have to discuss it, let alone investigate it, because those things are well-known and they could be seen.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: In your answer, Dr. Lukic, you said that "Mr. Ostojic is the last person who can interpret the government's decision." In fact, a few months before he made this speech at the Assembly, he was tasked, together with Mr. Brdjanin, by your government to, in fact, prepare the programme for the accommodation of refugees in the Republika Srpska, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The programme for the accommodation of refugees but not on that basis. A lot of officials were living in rented accommodations. They had to live somewhere, and on the basis that you're trying to impose on me which is to say that it was the -- it was Ostojic's policies, the government's policies, the policy of Republika Srpska, i.e., ethnic cleansing. You can look at the situation as it is today and you will see how many people returned where. You will see that the situation was not the way you tried to portray it, how many people we accommodated despite all the problems that we faced at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So you agree that Mr. Ostojic was tasked by the government to prepare the programme for the accommodation of refugees. We've seen now two Assembly sessions where Mr. Ostojic stated clearly that the policy was about the ethnical-geographical continuity of the Serb population. You were present at both of these sessions. You were the prime minister. But you never stood up at either of these sessions and said: No, no, no, Mr. Ostojic has got it all wrong, that's not the policy of my government, did you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're ignoring the fact that we were living in war time. There was a civil war going on. It was a war in which it was very difficult to make the right decisions in all of the cases; however, a large number of the people whom I know very well, both in the government and in the Assembly, did not accept the fact that we should throw out people and bring people in their stead. We tried to deal with the problems of the Serbs, of the Muslims, and of the Croats. I know of a lot of cases where we put up Croats and Muslims in a different apartment while we were waiting for his own apartment to be vacated. And it was not easy to vacate any of the apartments because everybody carried arms at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: In your answers, Dr. Lukic, you've continued to insist that the leadership called for the return of ethnic Muslim and Croat refugees to the RS, but in fact the Republika Srpska leadership, while it was seeking to populate empty areas of the RS with Serbs, was also working to prevent the return of Muslim and Croat refugees, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, in Bosnia and Herzegovina there is not an ethnically pure area where there were only Muslims who were chased away or Serbs who were chased away or Croats who were chased away. The population was mixed everywhere, and when you were talking about some of the regions I know that there were a lot of Croats and Serbs living there who were either chased away or they were killed. Please, you do not say that Serbs were killed in Lima, in Duvno, and Kupres at the very beginning of the war, in Brod, Sijekovac, and Samac. Who could we have settled there? The Serbs who had been killed? You do not mention that at all, and you keep on insisting on us taking a Muslim or a Croat apartment from them. At the same time they were allowed to return while those who had been living in their apartments were asked to move out. I repeat for the umpteenth time that a majority of the Serbs were chased away from the cities where -- they even had a large share, percentage share, and they had to move out to Serbia and many found their abodes in third countries. I repeat once again and I claim, take a cross-section. You will see that the Serbs in Republika Srpska returned more property to Muslims and Croats than it was done in the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It is a fact. I'm not making things up. These are the facts.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Could we go to P1385, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And this is the transcript of the 37th Assembly Session from the 10th of January, 1994, and, Dr. Lukic, the records indicate that you were present. You speak at this session and the minutes which are P1384 indicate that you were present. And if we could go to page 126 in the English and page 94 in the B/C/S. The context of this discussion is the -- the Assembly is at this point debating the report on the Geneva and Brussels Conference and defining a platform for further negotiations, so it's a discussion of the latest negotiations. And this is about the middle of the page in the B/C/S and it's right at the bottom of the page in the English. This is Mr. Vojislav Maksimovic speaking and he says: "What I would really like to see here is a firm attitude that the Muslims and the Croats will not be allowed to return to the areas under our rule. Accordingly, we should not return to the areas that will be under the Croatian rule. I think we should be decisive about this. Otherwise, I'm afraid that those people from Sandzak will occupy Srbinje and surrounding areas because there are too many of them in that area. So we should take a firm position and ban any of their returns to the territories we have gained through these international combinations." If we could go to the next page in the English and this is towards the bottom in the B/C/S. A few lines down he says: "I do not care if the Muslims will live at all, where they will live, whether they will have a country or not. I am not interested in that. The only thing I am interested in is my people and the territory where my people live. Therefore, any thought about having 500 or more Muslims within our future country is out of the question ..." And if we move down to the bottom of the page in the English, this is the next page in the B/C/S, Dr. Karadzic responds and he says: "What Mr. Maksimovic has said is correct. Yet, I must draw your attention to several things." And he speaks about the whole world being against them. And at the bottom of the page in the B/C/S and the next page in the English, in the middle of the page in the English he says: "Again, what Vojo has said is correct. My great-grandfathers are turning in their graves. All of my grandfathers fought against the Turks their entire lives, except my grandfather Stevan who fought against Germans." Just at the end of the page in the B/C/S he says: "As Vojo said, we are not creating our state, but instead we are constantly trying to patch together a piece of land for them and finally let them go. We cannot divorce from them. Our first strategic goal is to get separated from them. The world must allow us to do that ..." And he refers again to Mr. Maksimovic's speech at page 132 of the English and 98 of the B/C/S, and this is in the middle of the page in the English towards the bottom of the B/C/S he says: "As to the return of the refugees, I owe an answer to Vojo's question. According to the international law, we have no right to ban the return of the refugees. In principle, all refugees can return, but I would just add one sentence: 'This also has to be a two-way process.' The Muslims and the Croats accepted the two-way process. Later on Owen asked me: 'Why did you insist on the two-way process?' But when the Serbs from Zvornik return to Zenica, then the Muslims from Prijedor will return to Prijedor; therefore, it must be a two-way process. In accordance with the international law, we cannot declare a ban of the return of refugees." Dr. Lukic, what Dr. Karadzic is saying here in response to Mr. Maksimovic is that although it's impermissible under international law to ban the return of Muslims and Croats, he had insisted on a two-way process, conditioning the return of Muslims and Croats to the RS on the return of Serbs to Federation areas. And this was Dr. Karadzic's cunning way of limiting the return of Muslims and Croats to the RS, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dear Madam Prosecutor, if you knew what the Serbs suffered during the First World War at the hands of the Muslims, and I'm speaking now only about Muslims, and then during the Second World War, if you will believe me, I was only 8 years old when I watched the killing of 5,500 Serbs and 50 Jews. I was an 8-year-old boy. And then the rest that I experienced during the war would take us a long way and you wouldn't have any easy time listening to me. So what was done in the previous wars had created hatred not just on one side, on all the sides. And I can tell you that it was only Dr. Karadzic's wisdom that could deal with that and the principle of reciprocity was build into this. What's wrong with saying: Gentlemen, allow the Serbs to return to the territories from which they had fled and then we will allow people to return to our parts? But nobody respected that. In Mostar the Muslims and the Croats split the city and the Serbs are no longer there, and if you just look at Mostar you will understand the return in Bosnia and Herzegovina and the relationships there. On the other hand, I suppose that you do not believe that we always agreed at Assembly sessions. There was a lot of discord. Many times we kept our mouth shut, but when it came to the crunch we did only the things that were right. And I claim that not only the government but also the Presidency headed by Radovan Karadzic and the Assembly never took decisions that would result in crimes, irrespective of the fact that there were people, there were individuals, who were very radical there and so on and so forth. I really, really implore with you to bear in mind the developments that preceded our bloody war, and it seems that the origin of the evil is somewhere else. In the previous war, Serbs did not want to re-live the Second World War. For 15 years I've been the president of the association of Jasenovac/Donja Gradina. I am the leader of that association and I apologise for what I'm going to say. Jasenovac was the third-most notorious camp in Europe and in terms of monstrosity. It was the first in Europe and it was set up to deal with Serbs, Jews, and communists.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the gentleman please repeat the numbers of the people who died in Jasenovac.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you really think that it was not possible that it had an impact, not just any impact but a huge impact on the Serbs. I did not tell you anything about Prijedor. My father himself liberated Prijedor on two occasions, and he knows what he found there. You have to believe that what was done in Kozarac during the Second World War had to have its result. I apologise for side-tracking, but I really see that I had to tell you how things were in our parts.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Dr. Lukic, you've raised the crimes in Prijedor during World War II a number of times, and in fact last week when I asked you whether you could confirm that the Muslims in 1991 were the largest ethnic group in Prijedor, you referred again to the terrible crimes from World War II against Serbs in Prijedor and you said that this caused a disbalance - I think probably "imbalance" would be the better word - in the ethnic make-up of Prijedor. That was at transcript page 38783. So given --

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, but I cannot hear well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have problems both with the transcript and with the LiveNote.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear poorly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At a convenient moment I would like to correct the transcript and we don't have LiveNote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think they have to re-start the programme. Shall we take a short break for five minutes? --- Break taken at 9.34 a.m.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May I correct transcript before Madam Gustafson starts?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will speak Serbian. On page 12, lines 15, 16, the witness said "Serbs, Jews, and Roma" and not "communists". After that he said 700.000 Serbs, 25.000 Jews, and 80.000 Roma were killed at Jasenovac. We can check it with the witness if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Dr. Lukic, do you confirm having said so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Shall we continue, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Dr. Lukic, you've mentioned several times in your evidence the crimes against Serbs in Prijedor during World War II, and in fact last week you said that these crimes created an ethnic imbalance in the municipality. You've talked about the fact that these previous wars had caused hatred between the ethnic groups and about the fear among Serbs that these crimes from past wars would be repeated. Given all that, didn't you agree that in a place like Prijedor that it would be right to bring in ethnic Serbs to replace the Croats and Muslims who had left in order to correct this historical injustice and prevent these crimes from happening in the future?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, such a thing is impossible because I hope you believe me that I know that there is no way of destroying a whole people and wipe it out in a certain territory. I have mentioned the second -- World War II often probably, but at Kozarac there was a round table about the suffering of 59.000 inhabitants of Kozara. Among them there were also people from Prijedor. And whoever thinks that the consequences of previous wars, especially the Second World War, did not cause fear, that person obviously is unwilling to understand. What do you think why it was that I went to this war and my 20 or so close relatives? Not because they wanted to fool around there, but because they were willing to give their lives for their liberty and the liberty of their nearest and dearest. Many people suffered in Sarajevo, things happened that shouldn't have happened, but there was hatred. And when you were saying what was happening at our Assembly, well, if you knew what we heard had happened at the Muslim Assembly or the Croat Assembly, and -- because, you know, these were -- these things were linked. What the ones did affected the others too. Many intelligent people didn't accept many things, but they were silent. They kept silent. Fortunately, many things were not implemented because, after all, it wasn't possible to implement them.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'd like to go to 1D07862 now, please. And, Dr. Lukic, this is a document you discuss at paragraph 36 of your statement, and in general at paragraph 26 you asserted that Dr. Karadzic and yourself both insisted that every crime be prosecuted regardless of the ethnicity of the perpetrator. This is a document from the 6th of April, 1993, that -- written by you and it's sent to the Main Staff of the army and the command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. And in it you state that the government has been informed that there are cases of looting, killing, setting fire to buildings, and rape in the municipality of Novo Sarajevo, specifically Grbavica, committed mostly by members of the VRS. And at paragraph 36 of your statement you said that: "The government demanded that VRS crimes in Sarajevo should be prevented, and in this I have the absolute support of Dr. Karadzic, General Mladic, and General Galic." So I take it from this that General Mladic, Dr. Karadzic, and General Galic were aware that there VRS soldiers were looting, killing, setting fire to buildings and committing rape in Grbavica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask that we first check whether the witness has his statement in front of him; if not, he should. Apart from that, Madam Gustafson seems to be implying that these were crimes committed by the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm reading from the document which says the crimes were committed by the VRS. This is a document tendered by the Defence through this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, shall we continue?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Dr. Lukic, my question was: Given -- you've said that you had the support of Dr. Karadzic, General Mladic, and General Galic in these efforts. I take it that these -- General Mladic, Dr. Karadzic, and General Galic were all aware of these crimes being committed by VRS soldiers in Grbavica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, there were crimes. There's no doubt about that. I can say that it's hard to establish that it was done by soldiers. There would have been soldiers there but there would also have been rogues who went about and did nasty things, tortured women, and so on. There was one guy - I hope I needn't mention his name - who mistreated women and didn't care who they were. He was transferred to a territory where there were no women at all, but he continued and then he was killed by our own soldiers. I heard from the soldiers from where he was transferred that they think they should have done it themselves. Now some people are being tried, but I must tell you one thing, that's for sure, that there were many rumours and it seemed that more was happening than was actually happening --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Dr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- of course we know some people who came to harm this way --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Dr. Lukic, I'm going to bring you back to this document. You're writing to the commander of the Main Staff and the commander of the SRK about a very serious subject, about terrible crimes being committed by members of the military. Now, I take it that you would only have taken such a step if you had reliable information, as this document says you have, that these crimes were, in fact, being committed by members of the VRS; right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's done in peace time. In war time, even suspicions are checked. I got information that some bodies of ours were keeping camp. I wrote a letter, but later when I checked I found out it was false, that there was no camp there, that nobody had been detained, but I got such information anyway. In war time information is often sent out and it circulates, but it must be checked. And if you're asking me whether there was such things at Grbavica, well, at no place was there more of that than Sarajevo. And let me tell you also that more Serbian women were mistreated in Sarajevo than of -- than women of any other ethnicity. And I was in a position where I could come by information.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, in fact, Dr. Lukic, your concerns about the crime in Grbavica at this point in time were related to the fact that even the Serb population were becoming victims. In other words, it wasn't just Muslims and Croats who were being victimised. Even Serbs were becoming victims and that was your concern; right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Did you hear my question?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Half of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: My question was: Your concern at this point in time about crime in Grbavica was the fact that it wasn't just Muslims and Croats who were victims, but even the Serb population in Grbavica was being victimised; right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may seem that way when looked upon from these desks, but if you find yourself in a war, in war time chaos, it looks different. And it's difficult to say who may become a victim next. So, Madam Prosecutor, I was living in a peaceful building without knowing that 50 metres from there there had been armed Muslim soldiers for months but in civilian clothes. And that was close to a student hostel. I know that many of my friends came to harm and that was before --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Dr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- any Croats or Muslims or Serbs -- but I cannot give you an overview of an entire neighbourhood with some 10- or 12.000 inhabitants, or even more.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Could I have P1474, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And, Dr. Lukic, if I could ask you again to please try to focus your answer on the specific question I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I can hear poorly. The volume is very low.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Is that better now, Dr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's better.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to page 157 of the English and page 159 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Dr. Lukic, this is a military notebook from -- of General Mladic's and the entry I'm about to show you is from about two weeks before you wrote the document we just saw. It's dated the 25th of March, 1993, and you can see the title is: "Meeting with Prime Minister Lukic." And the second underline near the bottom of the page says: "Problems: "Theft, profiteering, looting, and desire to acquire wealth." And on the next page it says in the middle of the -- in the middle of the page: "Some soldiers rape even Serbian women (in Grbavica). (Lukic) himself took someone who had done this out of Sarajevo (he wouldn't say his name)." Now, Dr. Lukic, these notes reflect your concern that it wasn't just Muslims and Croats who were being victimised by soldiers in Grbavica. Even Serbs were victims; right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, come on, don't make up things. I am from Grbavica. I escorted dozens of girls of other ethnicities to Belgrade. I asked our soldiers to guard the Muslims where they were because where I was there was no one to guard them, to keep them safe. I made use of my connections to transfer Muslims from Petrovic to Belgrade and not only one, a great number, Madam. So if you -- if you're asking this question to me, then you're asking the wrong person. I know a number of people who did very similar things to what I did. For that reason, your question is an insult to me. If I may add, what would you do if a mother came to you with her 16-year-old daughter and asked you to save her? And there were many such -- nobody's protected in a war and there is no amnesty for anyone. And everything is done on a scale. On the one hand there is Sarajevo, on the other hand there is Srpsko Sarajevo. A shot from here, a shot from there, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If I could have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether the witness understood your question. What did you understand Ms. Gustafson's question to be, Mr. Lukic? Do you agree that you met Mr. Mladic on this day and having a word --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see that I did. I have no reason to doubt the content of Mr. Mladic's notes. But talking about such meetings with the leading people of municipalities and so on, there were many such meetings. Of course I cannot remember all the details, but it's obvious that we did meet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But did you see his notation that you said -- you referred to some soldiers who raped even Serbian women in Grbavica? Do you remember having said that to Mr. -- General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I may have told him about the case that I have already mentioned to you. And the word "even", well, I don't really use it at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If I could have 65 ter 1D07894, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Dr. Lukic, this is a document you discuss at paragraph 91 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, do you have your statement with you, witness statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Thank you, Excellency. I just ask it would help him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do we have a hard copy? And in the meantime shall we continue?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: This is a, Dr. Lukic, 28th of June, 1994, letter from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia Committee for Gathering Information on Crimes Against Humanity and International Law to the investigating judge of the lower court in Prijedor. And you discussed this letter in your statement and you state that it "represents a demand that Serbs who had committed crimes in Prijedor should be questioned to determine their responsibility." And you added that the government called for everyone who had committed crimes to answer regardless of the ethnicity of the perpetrator. This letter itself doesn't say anything about the crimes in question being crimes committed by Serbs. So I'd like to ask you: What is the basis for your assertion that this letter related to crimes committed by Serbs?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Prijedor there was a group of criminals, I would call them. Looters looted whoever they were able to reach and robbed property, and then they mistreated women unselectively and there were then individual killings. Eventually there was a number of individual killings and our service discovered 11 of them. They were interrogated, indicted, and transferred to the judiciary by our services. What happened later, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, this document says that there is a letter enclosed showing which witnesses to interview and about which circumstances, although that enclosure is not included in the exhibit. And I'd like to go now to 65 ter 25003. And this is a letter dated a few days before the previous letter, also from the FRY Committee for Gathering Evidence on Crimes Against Humanity and International Law, to the Republika Srpska Committee for Compiling Data on Crimes Against Humanity and International Law. And it's from the same author, Mr. Ilija Simic, as the prior letter. And it states that: "As agreed with your Commission ... we propose that the Lower Court in Prijedor examine the following witnesses living in Prijedor and its surroundings ..." And then there is a list. So the first person is to be interviewed about the arrest of Serbs in Kupres; the second witness about his capture in Bihac; the third witness about the purging of Serbs in Livno. The next page in the English. The fourth witness about the arrest of a Serb in Livno; fifth witness, arrest in Slavonski Samac --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How can this witness answer questions about documents emanating from a judge in Belgrade? What has that got to do with him?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I think the connection to the prior document which was an associated exhibit tendered with this witness is crystal clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Since your questions were generally a bit lengthy and since the witness was not shown his statement, I'm not sure whether he understood your previous question really, whether these documents in particular referred to in para 91 of his statement was directly mainly or even partly to those crimes committed by Serbs. So I didn't hear his answer to your question. Could you put your question again, Ms. Gustafson?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Dr. Lukic, the previous document --

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, I must first say that as hard as I tried to remember, I still do not recall this document at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Do you have your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Paragraph 91.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we show him --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: The previous document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- the previous document, 1D7894. So here you say this document represents a demand that Serbs who had committed crimes in Prijedor should be questioned. Do you remember having said that in your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And then if you look at this document which is before you -- so the question was: On what basis did you conclude that this was directed to the Serb perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is there any information? Not all information came in in writing. Much information came in through different channels.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't follow your answer. In your statement explaining this document, you said this document represents a demand that Serbs who had committed crimes should be questioned. What's your basis for such a conclusion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, probably one of the organs or public servants or somebody else informed us that these -- that this is about Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This has again been interpreted. The witness said "we had information" a few lines up, and he did not ask is there any information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. If we could go to 65 ter 25003.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For the purpose of planning, Ms. Gustafson, since we are sitting in a regular sitting schedule, we'll have our first break at 10.20 for 20 minutes and the second one at 12.00 for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Lukic, this is a document dated a few days before the previous document from the same author, from the same body to the RS commission on compiling data for crimes against humanity and international law, and it proposes that the lower court in Prijedor examine the following witnesses living in Prijedor. And we had started going through the list. If we could go to the next page in the English. Entry number 6, this is a witness to be interviewed about crimes against Serbs in Livno. Number 7, crimes against Serbs in Bugojno. If we could go to the next page in the B/C/S. Number 8, purging of Serbs around Zenica; number 9, the same; 10, also crimes in Zenica; number 11, crimes against Serbs in Zagreb, and so on and so forth. If we could go to the last page in both languages just to see -- give you a chance to see the last entries, every single one of the witnesses to be interviewed, according to this document, by the lower court in Prijedor are witnesses to crimes against Serbs committed outside of Prijedor. So the details in this letter make clear that the letter you referred to in your statement has nothing to do with crimes committed by Serbs in Prijedor, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to admit that I did not understand your conclusion at all. When we spoke about Serbs in Prijedor, of course we had certain information about them, that they had committed crimes. The service arrested them, investigated the matter, and indeed was convinced that they had looted, mistreated people, even committed some murders, and that's why they were arrested and prosecuted. As for this letter where other witnesses are being asked for, what does that mean? That means that there is a suspicion that these people are linked to some of the crimes that are mentioned here. That is not an unknown thing. It is well-known that persons committed crimes and then fled to other places. Of course they were searched for and many saw justice, others did not, and that is how things go in war time.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Dr. Lukic, maybe I can try one more time. I was asking you about the document that you discussed in your statement from the FRY committee to the investigating judge in Prijedor, stating that there are a number of witnesses in Prijedor that need to be interviewed about crimes. You said that was a document dealing with crimes committed by Serbs. Now I'm showing you a document from a few days before from the same committee, saying: This is our proposal for the crimes -- for the witnesses to be interviewed by the lower court in Prijedor and they're all dealing with crimes committed against Serbs in other areas. So I'm putting it to you that the document you referred to in your statement has nothing to do with crimes committed by Serbs.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking, that statement is not correct. If we found out, if it had been reported to us that a group of Serbs had committed crimes, different kinds, they didn't really pick and choose who they would steal from, who they would kill even, which women would be mistreated, et cetera, and then if these people were indicted, prosecuted. This document that came from Belgrade that you referred to, that's a completely different document of a completely different nature. It has to do with the search for persons who committed crimes elsewhere, not in Prijedor. They didn't really have anything to do with Prijedor, they just happened to be in Prijedor. That's the point.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6344, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If it is convenient, shall we take a break, Ms. Gustafson?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Dr. Lukic, at paragraph 33 of your statement you discuss civilian prisoners and the exchange of civilian prisoners. And it is your position that civilian prisoners were a category of people who were reasonably suspected of committing crimes and you said that these prisoners were exchanged regardless of the seriousness of the crimes of which they were suspected "because we wanted to save Serbian civilians who had been imprisoned and terrorised in prisons on the Muslim side." If we could go to P2684, please. I'm going to show you a document and then ask you a question. This is an order from the intelligence section of the VRS Main Staff from the 3rd of October, 1994, and it discusses exchanges. And in the third paragraph from the bottom in the B/C/S and near the bottom -- the second-last paragraph in the English, Tolimir says: "It should be kept in mind that in the exchanges we received captured soldiers of the Republika Srpska while we mostly give them civilians." Now, you said that you were exchanging civilians in order to save Serbian civilians from the other side, but here General Tolimir is saying that civilians are being exchanged for Serb soldiers; right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Often in war one does not choose. One does what one has to do. For example, with the Croats after the cease-fire agreement in 1993 we exchanged all for all. Very often we would hand over a criminal, but we cared about getting other people saved, rescued. And I have to say that others, Muslims, et cetera, when we did not have firm, solid evidence of major crimes, we would exchange them; or to put it more precisely, release them thereby. So this was not an opportunity for us to think: Will we do this? Such a person has such weight and another person has another weight. Usually we did an exchange all for all or group for group.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to talk -- ask you about something else in your statement. At paragraph 56 you -- of your statement you said that the Muslim side in Sarajevo wanted to present themselves to the world as victims. And you said: "As was the case with Cerska and Srebrenica, although the Muslims had food and other reserves, they constantly presented a false picture that civilians had nothing to eat and had no water ..." and so on. I'd like to ask you about Srebrenica when you were prime minister. You didn't go -- when you were prime minister in 1993 and 1994, you didn't go to the Srebrenica enclave to see the conditions for yourself, did you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know Srebrenica from before the war because I did some work there, for example, building a tunnel. Also, we measured Srebrenica, so I know it. I covered at least 70 per cent of its territory of the villages there. During the war I toured Srebrenica from all sides, from Milici, Konjevic Polje, then Kravica, when that crime was committed by the people from Srebrenica against it, then Bakovici and of course down to Ljubovija, rather, Skelani. As for those crimes in the Second World War and in this war -- and in this war --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm going to interrupt you because you're not answering my question. When you were the prime minister, you didn't go into the enclave and see for yourself the conditions that the Muslim civilians in Srebrenica were living in, did you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not possible for me to go, and let me end by saying that because my comment would be very long.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, a witness in this case, Major Tucker, did go into the enclave when you were prime minister in March 1993, and these were his observations. This is P4203, paragraph 178. "The refugees in the streets had mostly not had any real food since they had fled from Kamenica, Cerska, or their villages to the south of Srebrenica. What food they had was mostly a sort of cake made from a type of yellow flower that was quite plentiful under the cover of the fir forests which covered most hillsides in the Srebrenica area. Water came from the river that flowed through Srebrenica, but was polluted with awful excrement, urine, washing water and oil. The most abiding memory from my early days in Srebrenica was the stench of unwashed, dirty, damp, and sweaty human bodies in extraordinarily crowded circumstances." Now, it's your evidence that the Muslims in Srebrenica, among other places, constantly presented a false picture that civilians had nothing to eat and no water and so on. So is it your position that forest flowers and contaminated water were adequate sustenance for the Muslim civilians in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You've inverted the situation. I spoke of Cerska and some other places, and we checked and we took some cattle that had been taken from our territories beforehand. As for Srebrenica, you would have to have the following in mind: Srebrenica was a protected area; however, Srebrenica non-stop created war around its territory. They had large numbers of troops and they did not feed their troops poorly, although I believe everything that the gentleman wrote. However, I know that they were supplied in an illegal way. All Serbs know that and they know how and UNPROFOR knows that full well too. On the other hand, at the most decisive moment they sent 5.000 soldiers to other theatres of war outside Srebrenica, and had they agreed to a cease-fire, had they surrendered their weapons, the people of Srebrenica would have certainly lived through the war better than anyone else, either on the Serb side or on the Muslim side. Quite simply, because of their leadership, they were not in a position to accept that. Some lost their lives too. Let me not mention to you some Muslims from Srebrenica who wrote statements or actually entire books about the suffering of Srebrenica at the hands of its own leadership.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Could we go to 65 ter 05907.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And this is an associated exhibit you discuss at paragraph 94 of your statement, Dr. Lukic. In your statement you discuss the fact that you were a member of the state delegation in Dayton, and you note that the document states that the delegation will stand by the strategic goals adopted by the RS Assembly. And if we could go to page 2 in the English, we can see that the document indeed states that the delegation is obliged to adhere to the strategic goals as set out in 1992 by the National Assembly of Republika Srpska. I take it from this document and your evidence that at this point, October 1995, you were familiar with the strategic goals of the RS Assembly; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I was not at that Assembly and it was only on the second day that I heard that I was chosen to go to Dayton. That is one thing. Secondly, what else could a person say, a person who is going on behalf of a people that had suffered so much? However, in terms of the general knowledge of this gathering that I highly appreciate, we all went to Dayton with requirements that were far higher than what was realistic. Thankfully, everybody lost a bit so we all remained dissatisfied. But a document was adopted that nevertheless did bring about peace. Nobody's wishes totally came true. Everybody was short-changed a bit, so that's how we've lived since.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry, Dr. Lukic, I didn't ask you about the negotiations at Dayton. I just asked you to confirm that at this time, October 1995, when you were sent to Dayton with the delegation you were familiar with the strategic goals created in 1992 by the National Assembly. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, we did not know. I said that I heard only later that I would be going to Dayton, and others who came, none of them had any principles and documents in their pockets that had to be abided by. We all wanted to get more and we got what was allocated to us. That's a fact. And to this day I'm saying from this particular position as well that it's a good thing that none of us were completely satisfied.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Dr. Lukic, when you went to Dayton with the delegation, were you familiar with the strategic goals of the RS National Assembly?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not familiar with that. I did not hear about that. No one discussed that. Once we boarded the plane, we started talking how, what, and so on and so forth, as you can all assume because you are going into a total unknown.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Is it your position that when you went to Dayton you had never heard of the strategic objectives of the RS Assembly?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These strategic objectives were adopted in Banja Luka, allegedly. I was not present. I first read -- well, it was the very end of 1993 or the beginning of 1994, but I have to say to you that no one talked about them very much because war developments do not really take into account some kind of plans that you adopted at some session somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So is it your evidence that you first read the strategic goals of the Serbian people at the end of 1993 or the beginning of 1994? Have I understood your answer correctly?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. And I publicly stated that at another venue. Let me not bore you with all of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. If we could go to P1379, please.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: This is not discussed in your statement, Dr. Lukic. There's a document that's going to come up on the screen. This is a document we've seen several times now. It's the 34th Assembly Session that you were present and spoke at, and if we could go to page 14 of the English and page 13 of the B/C/S. This is Dr. Karadzic giving a -- more or less an introductory speech. And about halfway down the page in both languages he says: "Strategic goals adopted by this Assembly have been or will be achieved to the fullest extent just to remind those who do not know it. The Assembly reached strategic goals of Serb people which have become, in a certain way, our tasks, our obligation to realise them ..." And then he goes into a discussion of each of the goals. He talks about the first goal, the second goal, third goal, fourth goal, fifth goal. He explains what they are. And at the next page he mentions the sixth goal, an exit to the seaside. And then he goes on to discuss at greater length the fifth, sixth, and fourth strategic goals. Now, you were at this session, Dr. Lukic. Does this remind you of the fact that you would have been familiar with the strategic goals at this time, and indeed this is more or less consistent with what you said a few moments ago, at the end of 1993? Do you remember this speech of Dr. Karadzic's discussing the strategic goals?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say that I do have some idea about things being said. I remember very well the access to the sea that we negotiated in Dayton. We offered 48 square kilometres of the municipality of Trebinje in order to have access to the sea by Montenegro, Prevlaka Molunat, that part towards Dubrovnik. These were some excerpts, but I've been saying that I really did read this in the Official Gazette or somewhere, these principles, but that's roughly when I read it. And on some occasion, everybody talked about one of these objectives or the other in terms of the wishes that people had in terms of this war, and any country would like to have access to the sea. Why would Republika Srpska be short-changed in that respect because, after all, in our common state, Yugoslavia, we did have access to the sea.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. If we could go to 65 ter 25107, please. And, Dr. Lukic, you mentioned in your statement, although you didn't discuss the contents, you mentioned that you testified in -- in the Serbia versus Bosnia case at the International Court of Justice. And this document is a verbatim record of your testimony in March 2006. And it's only available in English. I will read the relevant parts to you. If we could go first to page 11.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I testified in the case of Bosnia and Herzegovina against Serbia as a witness on the side of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Right. And here at the top of the page it says that the first witness to be called by Serbia and Montenegro is Mr. Vladimir Lukic. You were then called upon to take a solemn declaration, and you state: "I solemnly declare upon my honour and conscience that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth." And if we could go to page 26. And this is when you were cross-examined by counsel for Bosnia, Ms. Korner, and she is asking you, in fact, about the strategic goals. And about halfway down the page

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER SAYS
utterances.text: "Yes, quite. Karadzic set out, didn't he ..." and she's talking about the 12th of May, 1992, Assembly "the six strategic goals of the Serbian people at that Assembly? The answer to that is 'yes' or 'no,' please." And then you answer: "First of all, I was not present at that session so I cannot say, because I do not know who said what, who proposed what, and who commented what." And Ms. Korner says: "Please, Mr. Lukic, are you telling us you did not know about the six strategic goals?" And you answer: "Madam President, honourable Judges, and Members of the Court, only two months ago or maybe three months ago, I read the text of these strategic goals. I really do not know how it came about that these goals should be formulated, but what I knew is that I discussed at one point these issues with General Mladic. Because he was asking me and asking the Government, in effect, to give them the idea, the goals, for the army to follow, meaning how far they should go - the army. Of course, I immediately reported it to Mr. Karadzic, but he simply actually did not say anything about it. He said nothing and he did not actually inform me that something of that sort existed, so I remained unaware of these goals until two months ago."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "So you never saw them when they were published in the Official Gazette?" And your answer: "Only two months ago." Now, Mr. Lukic, what you told the ICJ in 2006, that you'd only heard of the strategic goals two months before is a lie, isn't it, because you've said quite clearly to this Court today that you read the strategic goals in late 1993 or early 1994?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to intervene, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What's the point, Mr. Karadzic? Just a second --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The point is that the questions are full of falsifications. The gentleman read it two months ago. The witness is put in a very difficult situation here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, I think the witness is able to and should be able to answer the question. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First and foremost, I did not attend that Assembly session. I did not participate. I don't know -- I didn't know about that. I believe that what one can hear is something that can be discussed, but please I interpreted and I told you approximately when it was that I read those principles, as it were. And I can't give you the exact date or month. I can't do that because it was a long time ago. In other words, the fact is that I did not attend that Assembly session, that I did not participate in that discussion, that later on I never read anything about that. And this is an explanation given by President Karadzic and this is what General Mladic asked me and that's how things were. Everything else after such a long time would be pure speculation.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Dr. Lukic, you said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Let me intervene. The question was not whether you attended the session where strategic goals were discussed or set out, but when you read that strategic goals for the first time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that what I said at the court -- I believe that it was a couple of months before that that I had read it. But I don't know when and I wouldn't even be able to interpret those goals as I sit here today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But, Dr. Lukic, a minute ago when answering the question from Ms. Gustafson you answered like this. It's page 33, line 1: "These strategic objectives were adopted in Banja Luka, allegedly. I was not present. I first read -- well, it was the very end of 1993 or the beginning of 1994, but I have to say to you that no one talked about them very much ..." And you went on. So you clearly said you first read them in -- at the end of 1993 or the beginning of 1994.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that I made a mistake having said that. At the Tribunal here in The Hague I gave you the exact point in time when I had read them. My memory was still fresh at the time, so could you please take that as my statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Back to you, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. One last question on this topic, Dr. Lukic. I also read to you or showed you a long discussion of Dr. Karadzic's in 1993 about the strategic goals at a session you attended and you expressed your familiarity with that. Do you now want to change your evidence on that point as well and claim that you were no longer -- that you were actually not familiar with that speech of Dr. Karadzic's in 1993?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In general terms, I'm familiar with it, but I'm not familiar with the details thereof. Our sessions were sometimes long, there were a lot of items on their agenda, so it was impossible to retain everything that you heard at the session.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karadzic, you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Excellency. I would like to clarify some things just briefly and then I would like to shed light on some of the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Lukic, let's start with last things first. Can you tell the Chamber when it was when you heard of the strategic goals and then when it was when you actually read them?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know, it's very difficult to pin-point the time. I heard of them somewhat earlier, perhaps sometime when I became prime minister or somewhat later perhaps. However, I remember that after that conversation with General Mladic which was noted here as well, I saw that they actually existed, that a certain document did exist. Obviously I spoke to some other members of the government, members of parliament as well, but I remember your presentation most of all. But I don't remember the details of that presentation, of that speech, that you gave. And when I read the Official Gazette, finally then I saw the details of that document. Up to then, I really wasn't aware of all the details. I did not have them at my finger-tips.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who was the head of the delegation of Republika Srpska in Dayton?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The head -- or rather, the head of the entire delegation that we participated in was President Milosevic. And as for the part of the delegation representing Yugoslavia, there was also a delegation of Republika Srpska and its head was the speaker for the parliament, Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Besides having been prime minister, your profession as an expert in geography, did it play a role when you were appointed to the commission?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a professor in geophysics sciences.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I had been the director of the Republican GD 2nd Administration for nine years. For seven years I was the head of the institute. For 20 years I had measured Bosnia and Herzegovina and I knew Bosnia and Herzegovina very well. And on the other hand, I was also very familiar with some other relations. For example, in the entire republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina I was familiar with the structure of the population in certain municipalities, even in many of the villages there and so on and so forth. So I can tell you that our former opponents often asked me about certain things and not only about those things that were of service to our side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If 65 ter 05907 has not been admitted, and this is the appointment of the delegation, I would like to tender it because it was mentioned in the gentleman's statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Was it not admitted?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I think it was admitted, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3607, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And I apologise for the interruption. I just note that I forget to tender the extracts from the ICJ testimony, which was 65 ter 25107, pages 1, 11, and 26.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit those two pages.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6345, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, three pages. Yes. Yes, I think the numbers were not assigned yet officially on e-court. That's why you mistook that it was not admitted. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I believe that it was among those numbers that were rejected when redactions were made.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Lukic, on page 30 you were asked about -- about P4203, about what Major Tucker said about the situation in Srebrenica. Do you remember, or rather, can you remember how many and what kind of epidemics broke out in Srebrenica during the war?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since during the Second World War I survived typhoid - and not just me but many other people and families, although many died as well - I was always afraid of contagious diseases and epidemics throughout the war. And that's why I tried to have epidemics closely followed, not only on our side but also on the side of our enemy. And I must state that from what I heard and from what I learned from various channels, there was not a single territory of any of the sides, there were no war epidemics which are well-known from the previous periods, and that also includes Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 25 you were asked about a letter sent by Judge Simic. Was that the only letter that was sent to the commission, not to you, but to the commission? Was that the only letter he ever sent you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whatever, no. There were a lot of letters left, right, and centre. Everybody wrote, everybody had requests, everybody had proposals. We discussed a lot of those things; however, many of the letters, proposals, suggestions, complaints, both realistic and non-realistic, were in constant circulation. They were always there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The 11 people who were arrested in Prijedor, what was their ethnicity? What was the ethnicity of the perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly; however, I remember certain things from what I read or from what somebody told me. They were not Serbs, all of them, nor were those who were murdered and plundered all Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 18, Ms. Gustafson implied that you reacted to crimes in Grbavica only when the Serbs started suffering as well; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, it's not true. It is not true. Indeed, it is not. We reacted when humanitarian aid was not distributed evenly to everybody. I can tell you that when it comes to the distribution of that humanitarian aid and seeking routes for it to be delivered to the centre of the city and Grbavica, I co-operated with UNPROFOR. I got into their vehicles and drove around. We often reacted when it was not distributed to everybody. I'm sure that you will also remember that people did not receive pension monies. We reacted then as well. We know some of the municipalities' decisions. Some municipalities declared a state of war, whereas some annulled court decisions, for example, for a Serb who had committed a crime against a person of a different ethnicity, and we reacted then and so on and so forth. Mr. President, as a republic we functioned as a confederation of municipalities, a confederation of war municipalities in that. It is a notorious fact. That's what existed during the war. I have to say that we had municipalities which were better off than the republic itself, and with those people from those municipalities you could discuss everything but the budget. They would not allow us to come close to that budget at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were asked about Prijedor as well as to -- and that's on page 40, lines 14 through 18, and I'm going to read it in English. Page 14, lines 14 through 18. [In English] "Given all that, didn't you agree that in a place like Prijedor that it would be right to bring in ethnic Serbs to replace the Croats and Muslims who had left in order to correct this historical injustice and prevent these crimes from happening in the future?" [Interpretation] You were shown a map as well depicting the shooting range. Let me check the map number. Please bear with me. A map showing that there were Muslims in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to call up P783. P783.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was no interpretation. The upper left-hand corner, can it be zoomed in? Is there no interpretation into English?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at the map. There are markings for Muslims, 44 Muslims; 42 Serbs; and six Yugoslavs. In your view, who was a majority in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember and you could tell that in terms of the number of deputies, Prijedor and Sanski Most before the war were both Serb cities. They had a Serb majority. This is not how you do -- you colour a map. It all has to be green and the percentages have to show shares. This is not how you colour a map. However, I don't want to talk about Prijedor, Sanski Most, and others because I would take up too much of your time, and the stories would be ugly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we now look at the statute which is 1D9100. We will have to put it on the ELMO. Let's look at the statute of the municipality of Prijedor. Before the elections in 1991, we're talking about the statute which was issued by the communist Assembly. Let's put it on the ELMO. I'm interested in page 1 first and then I will be looking for page 2, Article 6. Professor, could you please read the heading and the decision on the changes to the statute and then we will go to page 2 where I'm interested in Article 6. Do you see the preamble?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please read it out aloud.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Pursuant to Article 239 and 301 of the Statute of the Municipality of Prijedor, the Official Gazette of the Municipality of Prijedor. Issue number illegible, the 7th of 04, 985, the Assembly of the Municipality of Prijedor at the joint session of all councils, dated 14th September, 1992, issued a decision on the changes of the statute of the municipality of Prijedor."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please read slowly and can we now see page 2, Article 6, please. Slowly.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "In the statute of the municipality of Prijedor, Article 208 or perhaps 206 through 212 is hereby raised and in the provisions of the articles of the statute the word 'delegate' is changed into the word 'deputy', whereas the word 'delegation' shall be deleted. Article 6 --"

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Slowly, slowly.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The word 'composition' and the appointment of the council before Article 223 shall hereby be deleted and Article 233 is changed and from now it shall read" --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You are reading too fast.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The Assembly of the municipality of Prijedor is a --" I can't read, "has one house and 90 deputies of whom 41.59 per cent are of Serbian ethnicity and 38.7 are of Muslim ethnicity, whereas 6.7 are of Croatian ethnicity. There are 9.70 per cent Yugoslav and 3.31 per cent of other nationalities and national minorities in proportion to the ethnic structure of the population of the municipality of Prijedor."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So who was a majority on the eve of the elections? What would you say?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no doubt about that. I knew that even earlier because I did have some information, and there can be no doubt that Prijedor and Sanski Most had a Serbian majority and that a number of municipalities by the Sava also had a Serbian majority. Some Posavina municipalities were mentioned as scarcely having any Serbian population at all, but that's not true. There were some municipalities with a significant share of Serbs and some even had a Serbian majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do take a look at Bosanski Brod which is marked as Croatian. 34 per cent of Serbs and 12 per cent of Yugoslavs, right, or Muslims. 30 per cent of Yugoslavs?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mentioned municipalities by the Sava. Is this one?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. Nobody wants to admit, but about 60 to 80 per cent of the population in any municipality who declared themselves to be Yugoslavs were really Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted and marked for identification?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D3620, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, about the map we just -- we are seeing now, I don't see there's any translation for the legend. Probably we need it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: We'll take care of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Professor, did you know that before the war and even during the first months of the war there was a discussion about talks according to which each ethnic community should establish their municipality and that this also applied to Prijedor offering the Muslims to establish their own municipality?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: That was an absolutely leading question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How else can I put it? This is generally known to the Chamber and everybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were there any discussions? How else do I phrase it? Was Prijedor also one of the cases in which there should have been two municipalities?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were many municipalities in which there were balanced shares of different ethnicities, and in those municipalities a division was envisaged along ethnic lines. As far as I know, Prijedor was one of these but I'm not sure. I would say yes, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then what can you say about the suggestion of the OTP that it was the government's plan to settle Serbs in Prijedor with the implication that they would be settled in Muslim villages?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm really not a person who thinks that you can compensate for one crime with another crime. I'm on the side of truth and truth can never lead to crime.
