Moving one group out, moving another group in, and kill the ones so that the others may live, such options don't stand a chance. And eventually that was the option of those who began the war with massacres such as those that they were committing during the previous war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were asked about document 1D5756. You were asked about your attitude toward minorities, your opinion about settling, about relations toward other communities, so could we please see the document that I mentioned?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which page is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The document number is D7856. It's about a government session. Actually, it's admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That was discussed in your statement in paragraph 27.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see that it was admitted subsequently, so we don't have to ... During the break some documents were admitted so we must fix that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting, you said, Professor, that there were extreme positions in discussions even at government sessions. So let me ask you if there is a single document which was adopted based on these extreme positions or angry discussions by some delegates?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of a single instance of such an extreme attitude being adopted, be it at government sessions or at Supreme Command meetings and so on. And, Your Honours, in such a war which was a civil war and a religious war, extreme positions actually nurture each other. Because when we try to calm somebody, their reply is: But don't you know what the others did or said? And so on. It's best to avoid such situations, keep silent, and then do it your way and do it differently. In war this can be useful.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. A good part of the cross-examination was about our attitude toward minorities, especially Muslims. Could we please see 65 ter 05985 which you mention in paragraph 41 of your statement. This is the 68th Session of government from the 22nd to the 26th of April at Bijeljina. Could we please see page 5 -- paragraph 4, that is, at 4. 4 in English, please. I don't know which page it is. In the proposed text the bill was -- could we please see item 4 in English. It must be on the following page. Could we please see item 4 in both Serbian and English. It starts at the bottom of the page in Serbian, and in English it must be on the following page. [In English] Next page, please, next page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Next page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think we have only two pages in English, which is a partial translation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we get the following page in Serbian?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Lukic, did you have any co-operation with Herceg-Bosna and did you enable their high officials to come to Republika Srpska to see for themselves how the Croats were living there?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was in April 1993, but give or take one month, owing to your agreement with the president of Herceg-Bosna and with my agreement with the prime minister of Herceg-Bosna whom I had known from before the war for -- and I had a positive opinion of him, we made an agreement to cease hostilities. We made an all-for-all exchange of prisoners. We allowed them to come to our territory and see how their people, or rather, people of Croatian ethnicity were living. And to my mind what was very good was when the Croatian side was in a position to lose more, even a couple of dozen thousand people because they were in a serious conflict with the Muslims, you remember well that we let entire formations and a huge number of people to move from the upper part of the Bosna and the middle part of the Bosna River to go to their territories and I'm convinced that's when we saved thousands of people from being massacred. Mr. Prlic and I were trying to get the Muslim side interested to accept the cease-fire to stop the war, and the talks may have yielded some results. Unfortunately, the Muslims didn't accept, they didn't want to hear of it, and I'm still sorry that it didn't happen. But what we did in respect of the Croats - and you remember that our hospitals were also full of wounded Croats - we let many of them cross over and we assisted them in every way. Of course they also paid us back in some cases. What certainly is true was that the Muslim side accepted then but they were striving to reach an achievement -- an agreement in Washington for the Croats and Muslims to unite again against the Serbs and that war should be continued with the assistance of NATO and so on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see 1D2941, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we move from this document, I want you to clear what the status of this exhibit. This was admitted, I mean 5985. This was part of the associated exhibits referred to in paragraph 41, and in paragraph 41 referred to items 2 and 27. But what was translated is only item 2 but not 27. So probably put this marked for identification pending the English translation of item 27 as well. Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency. That's exactly it. Item 2 was also tendered. So could we please see 1D2941. And I apologise because I did not expect our attitude toward minorities to be put in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please read the first two sentences from the top. Do you recognise this photograph and do you remember this occasion? Is this that visit on the 4th of October?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's go to the top of the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please read the first two sentences.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "My wish to visit Banja Luka to convince myself that Croatian people live here was realised today because political conditions in that regard have been established. Serbs and Croats in these areas did not wage war. The majority of Croats remained in Banja Luka which is as a result of a positive attitude of the Republika Srpska. Therefore, the departure of Croats from these areas should be prevented. In other words, the vacating of the apartments which should be regulated by law." This was said by Jadranko Prlic, the president of Herceg-Bosna whom I mentioned a few minutes ago. I had known him from before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What kind of a reaction did this provoke on the Croats in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reactions were mostly positive, although some could be negative too. It wasn't always harmonious. It was not all wine and roses. The majority of politicians, however, understood that this was the direction to move in and this also gave us strength to continue working in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this please be admitted for identification? Oh, sorry, there is a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, my issue with this document is it appears to be a part of an article that's literally been cut out of a newspaper and put onto this sheet. We'd like to have the opportunity to look at the whole article in its context and assess it and, indeed, see if there are any other portions of this particular article that should be included with this extract. In principle, I don't have a problem with this extract going into evidence in light of the witness's answers, but we would like an opportunity to review the entire article.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would suggest we admit the article and if the Prosecution has any other portions it would like admitted, we won't have any problem with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll admit this and you may come back if there's an issue in relation to this news clipping later on. Shall we give the number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3621, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, if it is convenient, the Chamber is minded to take a break, a bit longer break, till 12.30. Yes, we'll rise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Professor Lukic, nevertheless, did you and Jadranko Prlic manage to win over part of the Muslim population, or rather, some of the Muslim leaders for peaceful co-operation?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, Mr. Abdic, Fikret Abdic, and his part of the people. That's the Muslim people in Western Bosnia, mostly in the area of Kladusa. We had a few meetings with him and I must say that he was a great supporter of bringing the war to an end since he was supposed to be elected president of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Unfortunately, he voluntarily gave up on that office. During the war, we concluded through our talks with Mr. Abdic he was truly against the war. As a businessman he was well-known from earlier on. He was in favour of peace and tolerance among all ethnic communities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what is decisive there, with one Muslim orientation one could not establish peace and co-operate and with the other one one could?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously there was this orientation of Mr. Alija Izetbegovic in terms of this purely Muslim option, this Islamic state, I beg your pardon. And he could not give up on that, even at the cost of waging war. I think that the best example is the Cutileiro Plan that he did not accept. Basically he withdrew his signature. It no longer matters who talked him into doing that. However, during the war when on several occasions we tried to have some kind of contact at least, to fight less, if I can put it that way. Unfortunately, we did not quite succeed in that because, quite simply, he was in favour of creating an Islamic state in Bosnia-Herzegovina, no matter how big it may be, as he said on one occasion, even if it were as big as a small coffee cup. However, Mr. Abdic was a person with a broader outlook and indeed he made proposals to us. He thought that Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Boban and others who co-operated with them would manage to get something done in terms of softening this Muslim hard-line in order to reach a timely peace, most importantly to establish peace.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you briefly identify a document that we are going to have placed on the ELMO now, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May I ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you tell the Trial Chamber, as you look at the preamble and the heading, can you tell us what this is about?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the prime minister of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, Dr. Jadranko Prlic; the Prime Minister of Republika Srpska, Dr. Vladimir Lukic; and the prime minister of the Autonomous Province of Western Bosnia, Zlatko Jusic, MA, support the joint statement signed in Zagreb on the 21st of October, 1993, between the president of the Autonomous Province of Western Bosnia, Fikret Abdic; and the president of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, Mate Boban, MA; as well as the declaration signed in Belgrade on the 22nd of October, 1993, between the president of the Autonomous Province of Western Bosnia, Fikret Abdic; and the president of the Republika Srpska, Dr. Radovan Karadzic, as an expression of true will in favour of establishing lasting peace in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Well, yes, I do remember this full well and I think that this was indeed a high-quality document that would lead to ending the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. That was an opportunity if Croatia was ready to go for peace too, but I must say that despite all the talks we had and this document that you signed, unfortunately the war went on and you know until when and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please show the last page now so that the professor could identify the participants.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Jadranko Prlic was there, Vladimir Lukic, and Zlatko Jusic, Zlatko Jusic on behalf of Western Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you please lift this up a bit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And of course the president, Fikret Abdic, down here.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The microphone is switched off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, could you repeat.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted or marked for identification because I'm not sure that we have a translation yet?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is this a part of a book? Can we see the page numbers?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From some book, I don't know which one, but it is authentic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can we see the bottom? Yes. Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: It's a Prosecution -- I mean, it's a document from our evidence collection. I'm not -- I'd have to look into the source. I don't have an answer at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D3622, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were asked about war booty. Could you please tell the Trial Chamber how and in which way this question was regulated?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, war booty went through certain organs, and we also had legal regulations about that. Whoever obtains war booty is to hand it over to someone and also there are regulations on how it should be guarded and also how it can be used and for what purposes, depending on what the war booty actually is. So it had different purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did war booty include property that was seized, property that was legal and whose owner was known?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Private property could never officially, publicly, through certain organs, be included in war booty.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us about smuggled goods that were seized, cars of unknown origin, smuggled food, drink, et cetera? Could the state use that in a lawful way?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. Also people were looking at what it was, where it came from, and so on. Also, there were regulations in that field, how to deal with such property. In war if there is nothing else that gives a good yield, it is definitely smuggling that yields fruit and I think that that's a well-known thing here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were asked about Mico "Joje" and Mandic, how they sold Golf cars and it says somewhere that Radovan Karadzic knew about that. Did they sell that on their own behalf or did the state or government assign automobiles to their services, say the police and so on?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's a leading question very much. You could ask how could -- in which method, on what basis, did they sell those items. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it was suggested that they were selling them, but it wasn't said that they were doing it for private purposes. So it has to be specified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You are putting words to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I say something? Judge, sir, may I say something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the other day I wasn't clear enough when I spoke about this property. There was smuggling and there were other things. But as regards the problem of Golf cars and some other vehicles and so on and so forth, primarily this was given, or rather, the municipality, for instance, had a lot of vehicles and then they would let the ministries and other organs have some. As for these mentioned persons and these vehicles, it is correct that they exported some of these goods. They were sold, that is true, but this money was used for a particular purpose, for different purposes. For instance, you know that we had to take our wounded very far away because in Republika Srpska we did not have enough hospitals. So many vehicles were given to hospitals, ministries, and so on, for their use. In other words, these goods, in a way, had been taken but for a particular purpose and they were used for some general purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were asked, or rather, it was suggested that you believed that there should be a Serb entity and within that context it was necessary to have a corridor. Could you tell the Trial Chamber why the Serbs from the western areas did not use the Brotherhood and Unity Highway in that period of time?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could just specify the period of time with a date, I think that would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- may I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please wait. Mr. Karadzic, reformulate the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 53 you were asked, or rather, it was suggested to you that -- how you imagined the Serb entity, and in that context it was stated that you advocated the opening of a corridor. To the north of the Sava River between Zagreb and Belgrade there is a highway called Brotherhood and Unity. Why did the Serb side not use the highway? Why did they have to secure a corridor on the southern bank of the Sava River?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Gentlemen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. I couldn't find the reference, but Ms. Gustafson wanted to know the time-frame about -- that you are asking about.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was the previous day, sorry, rather, last week, page 53.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At the time when the corridor was created in the beginning of the war, June 1992, that's when the corridor was created and you explained that babies were dying and so on and so forth. So now I'm asking you whether that corridor was indispensable and why they did not use the highway?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now that the time-frame has been specified, I have an objection because the question is related to this witness's proposals to Dr. Karadzic about a corridor in the fall of 1991. And now he's being asked about why the corridor was opened in June of 1992 and the attempt is being made to link this back to his earlier answers. And I think that's confusing. The questions that I asked about the creation -- or his proposals for a corridor in 1991 were related to the contemplation of a separate Serb entity. It is now confusing to talk about the war situation in 1992 and the opening of a corridor at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I see her point that it's not directly related to that portion of the direct examination, so perhaps Dr. Karadzic can link it with another question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But a corridor may serve the same purpose irrespective of the time-frame. That's -- yes, Ms. Gustafson?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, in 1991 there was of course no conflict in Bosnia and in 1992 there was. So the corridor -- creating a corridor in 1992 when there are different parties with different -- with control of different parts of the territory, in my submission, is a completely different question from the creation of a corridor in 1991 before there is an actual armed conflict. And my questions were related to that pre-war scenario.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can rephrase --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber agrees with Ms. Gustafson's observation. Please move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to ask whether in 1991, or rather, in the autumn of 1991 something happened in Croatia because we could not use all the roads at that time -- but never mind. The last question, Professor: You were suggested that the Serbian Democratic Party fought to have influence on the government. Apart from you who were not an SDS member, were there any other ministers who were not SDS members or were members of a different party?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please don't take my word for granted. I believe that there were three or four other ministers who were either members of different parties or not party members at all. Mr. President, you asked me about something and I answered, but I would like to add something to my answer. I believe that a mistake was made so I would like to correct that mistake with your leave. And it's about the movement of vehicles and people around Bosnia and Herzegovina. May I be allowed to proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In late June or perhaps between mid-June and the end of June, on Mount Igman in 1991 we held a Yugoslav conference and that conference ended half a day earlier to allow people to go home. And we suggested the people from Serbia not to go down to the Sava River or take the highway. We told them to go across Mount Romanija, but I don't want to bore you with all the details. Therefore, the freedom of movement stopped existing as of May 1991 and connected to a lot of risk. Some people who took the highway never got home if they were on buses --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I don't follow. You wanted -- you said you wanted to correct your evidence. What was your mistake?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, it's not a mistake in my answer. I was referring to the fact that one could [as interpreted] move freely around Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia in 1991. I wanted to correct that statement. I wanted to add to that by saying that that was, in fact, not true.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Line 18, it shouldn't be "could" but "could not."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was the minister of veterans Dr. Dragan Djokanovic, while you were prime minister was he an SDS member? If not, what party did he belong to?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Dragan Djokanovic was the minister for veterans. He had his own party but I don't know what it was called. He had his own party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what about Mr. Kalinic, was he a member of the SDS at that time or was he a member of another party?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was still in Markovic's party at the time. You know it much better than I do. You know what party that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And my last question: Is it possible that one party which is in power allow for an embittered opponent to be appointed to a responsible position on its behalf?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not possible before the war or during the war. It is still not possible. It has never been possible at least in our neck of the wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And now on page 27, last week, line 6, you were asked a question which due to the double negation in our language and an impossibility to use that same negation in English it was not clear why you said "yes." The claim was your job was not to investigate and then you said: Well, yes. Does this mean that it was indeed your job to investigate or it wasn't?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What investigation do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It was about your term of office in the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I was not the one who investigated. As the developments unfolded, I had to record them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Thank you for having come to The Hague to testify and thank you for your co-operation. This will be all that I had for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That concludes your evidence, Mr. Lukic. On behalf of the Chamber, I thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be given the floor to say something? Would that be in order? Is it customary?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, Mr. Lukic. Please have a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to thank you. That was all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If the witness takes the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Poparic. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Poparic.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Before we start, if I may, I have to deal with the corrections.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll get there yet. But we have already noticed that both of us are speaking fast and don't make breaks. So I kindly ask you to pause between my question and your answer, and I remind both of us that we should speak slowly so that what we say might be interpreted and recorded. Now, although it's an integral part of your report, could you please introduce yourself to the Trial Chamber and tell us what your -- about your education and your career.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC
utterances.text: I am a mechanical engineer. I graduated from the school of mechanical engineering in Belgrade. I specialised in ballistics. I graduated from the department for ballistics, and it was the only school in the former Yugoslavia where one could learn about ballistics. Later on that was also taught at the military academy in Zagreb, and I believe that it exists in Belgrade these days. However, all the ballistics professionals had to graduate from that school in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you to slow down, please, if possible.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC
utterances.text: At the time when I was a student at that school you had to cover all the areas of weaponry - rocket weaponry, classical weaponry, ammunition, and assets. So my generation is the one that had -- that gained general knowledge. When I graduated from the school of mechanical engineering, I also completed the school for reserve officers in Zagreb. I underwent military training. I familiarised myself with all the types of weaponry in the then-Yugoslavia, both infantry and artillery weaponry. And after that I joined the JNA and I was assigned to work at the Pretis factory where I was involved in the construction of rocket projectiles and thereafter of artillery projectiles. In 1991 I was transferred as an officer to the technical testing centre where I remained working until the end of my professional career when I was pensioned off in 2007.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The technical testing centre is what we call TOC?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was the testing centre which tested all the assets that were supposed to become part of the standard catalogue of the JNA armament and later on of the JNA armament.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have a rank?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC
utterances.text: Yes, when I was pensioned off I had a rank of lieutenant-colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did your centre co-operate with Pretis; and if it did, up to when?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC
utterances.text: The TOC co-operated with Pretis always. That co-operation was never discontinued even during the war or after the war. I co-operated with my colleagues from the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina who still work in that institution and they still use certain of Pretis' services. I co-operated with them when I was still active. So the TOC co-operated with Pretis constantly during the war and after the war. I'm talking about this Pretis company from the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you were transferred to the TOC in Belgrade, did you get involved in expertise and did you participate in the testings that were subsequently used?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC
utterances.text: Yes, we were involved with expertise in the army, which means that all of the incidents that involved arms and ammunition had to be investigated and somebody from the TOC had to be involved. I participated in several such investigations, starting with the explosion in the Vranje depot, some incidents among the troops. I also worked for the military court in Podgorica, where I carried out forensic expertise as a member of the TOC. The TOC was tasked with that and I was the one who was actually the representative of the TOC that got the task. I did not even mention it in my CV because I didn't think it was important.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what was the relationship with with the TOC and the Nikinci testing ground?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC
utterances.text: The Nikinci testing ground is part of the TOC. I have to say that the TOC in the SFRY had several testing grounds that it used. One was in Prevlaka, another one was in Nikinca, and the third one was in Kalinovik. Occasionally we could use some army testing grounds as needed. The Kalinovik testing ground was a reserve testing ground in case of war. The TOC had its war assignment in Nevesinje and that's where the war reserves of the TOC were stored. I remember that we had some flak jackets there and during the sanctions I used them. Those had been transferred to the Republic of Yugoslavia and we used them. That -- those were war reserves in Nevesinje. The testing ground was in Kalinovik and the war reserves were kept in Nevesinje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell the Trial Chamber where are Nevesinje and Kalinovik and where were they then?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC
utterances.text: Throughout the war they were in Republika Srpska and they still are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up 1D28759. I believe that it has a D number but I don't have it. So I would like to call up 1D28759. Maybe it was not admitted. 1D28759.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you check the number again?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While you worked at Pretis and at the technical testing centre, the TOC, apart from specialising in projectiles, did you have an opportunity to familiarise yourself with all kinds of weapons and armaments that the JNA had?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely, during my work, my studies, and the reserve officers' school of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your report too the rule is mentioned for the sniping rifle, the mortar, that is, the rules of using these armaments. Can you explain what that means and what kinds of rules those are for individual armaments? 1D71 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 7902, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The rule that I cited is a basic document to be used by troops using any armament that is represented in the army. For example, this rule or manual for the sniping rifle contains all information those who need that rifle need to know. Talking about this rifle, how do you use it, what kind of sights are available, how snipers are selected, even the tests are described used to select snipers, and later they are trained and so on. Then there are firing tables and so on. For each asset there is such a manual and they're not all the same. Talking about the 82-millimetre mortar, well, that manual contains the same information as that for the rifle; that is, the parts, the advice for use, but also information regarding its positioning on the ground, how the elements for firing are calculated, and even information about the consumption of ammunition depending on the type of target and depending on your intention, if you want to warn the enemy or destroy the target. And whoever's in charge will decide about the use of the mortar and the way it is used. For example, if it's the commander's assessment that a target must be destroyed because of the danger it poses to that commander's unit, he can take such a decision. And then there are standard values for that kind of action. For one type of target, for example, you need 216 shells of 80-millimetre calibre. That's a target 100 to 200 metres wide and some 50 metres deep. And that is roughly the area covered by a squad, an assault squad. Of course a commander can deviate from these values. That's his discretionary right. In case of larger targets, we're also talking about a larger number of shells and so on. There are also rules in force for other assets and these rules describe in detail how the asset is used by troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In this indictment against me and my officers disproportionality is often mentioned. Can you tell us based on what we've just heard, 216 shells of 82-millimetre calibre rather than 80-millimetre as has been recorded, how is that determined? What does it mean to fire disproportionately if you need as many as 216 shells to destroy a target?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC
utterances.text: It's difficult to make such an assessment. Talking about a mortar, the commander has the right to assess that his unit is threatened and that the enemy position must be destroyed. Destruction means destroying over 50 per cent of the enemy's assets. It all depends on the situation. It's all part of the discretionary right of the commander, and everything else is really about fine-tuning and I cannot go into all the details. It all depends on the situation. Of course there are situations when many shells are used without that being considered disproportionate use. And the standards I mentioned are not peculiar to the JNA. Those are international standards. The JNA didn't invent new things in that respect. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm waiting for the transcript and I would also like to ask you to mind that.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I don't see the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us briefly see D3560. D3560. It was admitted through Witness Subotic. Could you please tell us if you are familiar with this or such a document and what does it mean?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is a standard request for testing at the Nikinci testing site -- test site. This is about 120-millimetre shell and a functional test is requested and an extreme temperature test. And below we see the composition of elements - the jacket, the primer, the basic charge, and so on. This is the typical way how ammunition was sent to Nikinci for testing and it shows that it was tested in accordance with the regulations about quality of products which define the conditions it must meet to be approved. The test institution conducts the appropriate tests, and in case all the test results are positive they make a relevant report and then that asset can be sent to the warehouses or the units and so on. This is from 1994 and it was signed by Miloje Jokic, the director of control. And this shows that during the war the control procedure was fully abided by at Pretis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us what this means, what we read here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. I wonder if we could just ask whether this document was cited in the witness's reports and where it was cited in the witness's reports, because otherwise I think we're a little bit at sea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Fair enough. Could you assist us, Mr. Poparic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can tell you specifically. This document is not cited in the reports. But since I worked on other reports with Mrs. Subotic too, I see it as a document which proves that at Pretis there was product control in place which was in line with the regulations. That was being contested specifically in the case of air bombs, that Pretis did not work in accordance with the technical documentation, regulations, and so on. However, this document shows that they did work in accordance with the usual way of manufacturing ammunition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I believe I can call up another document. You said you are familiar with the armaments held by the JNA. Could we please see 1D07465. It's a video-clip of the BH army which was put on YouTube. It's the 4th Motorised Brigade of the 1st Corps. It's from 00.2.35 to 00.2.55?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we take it that this is another item that was not cited in the witness's reports?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Poparic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It has to do with our reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry? While it has to do with your report, but it was not cited.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was not directly cited, but there are documents that are linked to this very video-clip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we start at 00.2.35 and go through 00.2.55.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please pay attention to the assets that can be seen there. 00.2.35.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure that we have seen everything.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I saw two assets. One was a multi-barrelled rocket-launcher, it has 12 barrels. It's a Chinese-made launcher of 107-millimetre calibre. It's a very well-known MLR. It was also manufactured in Iran and North Korea and many countries use it. The JNA never had such a launcher. It had a launcher which was produced more or less at the same time, in 1963, a 128-millimetre calibre launcher with 32 barrels. It was called Plamen. And the other asset was a 130-millimetre M46 gun with a maximum range of 27 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Poparic, I think you are speaking too fast.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat from the part where you said it was called Plamen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The JNA never had the multiple rocket-launcher 127-millimetres. This launcher is interesting for us because in the documents that were at our disposal in this case, there was a document issued by the KDZ of the BH MUP. And they analysed the traces after an explosion in the former Palmero Tojati [phoen] Street where one rocket from such a launcher hit a private apartment. It was their conclusion that the projectile had come from the direction of Ilidza and they also stated that the launcher -- that the JNA had such launchers, which is false. The launcher that we saw here on Igman didn't have a range as long as Palmero Tojati Street because its range is 8,500 metres. And the distance from Igman to that street is somewhat greater. So if the investigators established that it was fired from the direction of Ilidza, it could only have come from the Alipasino Polje industrial zone because, as I said, the JNA did not have such launchers and therefore I believe the VRS didn't have them either, at least I don't have any information to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In line 25, the previous page, it's not 127. You said 107, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm actually kind of wondering where we're going with this because this is the second item that was not referred to, footnoted, in the witness's reports. And expert or not, that doesn't relieve the Defence of their obligation to notify the Prosecution of documents that they might otherwise be using with the witness, especially when it's not been cited in their reports. And, with respect, I think we're on to an area that is completely irrelevant and far and away outside of the scope of the witness's report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I was wondering about the direction in which we are going. Mr. Robinson, do you want to say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. With respect to the relevance, I think this is an attempt to show that with respect to the incident in which the shelling -- shells landed in Alipasino Polje on the 22nd of January, 1994, that the origin of that fire was not from the Bosnian Serb side. With respect to the notice, however, that's I think our error, that if we're going to lead documents which are -- even though he's a viva voce witness, if we're going to lead documents in addition to those mentioned in his report, we should have given the Prosecution notice and I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given that Mr. Poparic is an expert, I expected Mr. Karadzic would lead evidence in order to tender his reports first. So I was wondering where are we heading to. And I'm not sure about the origin of this film as well. I don't think Mr. Poparic is in the position to give evidence about that. Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a film that is on YouTube. We can see here that it says "Patriotic League Video." This is a series of video films that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you involved in editing this page, filming of this? Do you know when this was filmed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This footage is part of a TV programme from 1993. It was shown on BH television. This is just a clip from that TV programme, and the entire video can be seen on YouTube and probably the entire video might even be here. This is a video that speaks about the 4th Motorised Brigade and its commanders speak themselves and so on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, because time is short I didn't want to go into specific incidents. I wanted to complete these general matters so that I can start with the incidents tomorrow and complete them tomorrow, I mean the ones that are contained in the findings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll admit those parts played. Shall we assign the exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3619, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could I now ask for 65 ter 24216.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: A moment ago you spoke about the roles and ammunition spent, so on this table could you explain that to us? Can you tell us what it actually shows?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The document that is on the screen at this moment, 65 ter number 24216, is not footnoted, as far as I'm aware, in the witness's reports for which he's the principal co-signatory -- pardon me, the principal signatory, and we've not been notified that this was going to be used. And as I said, we're still entitled to that notification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I was just telling Dr. Karadzic that he should at this point give the Prosecution all of the numbers of documents he intends to use during this examination. So I don't know if you want to have him do that orally or we can adjourn early for the day and we can give them that notice this afternoon so that they can be ready tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can he not deal with the -- his report for ten minutes and continue tomorrow with these documents?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can, but then I'd have to move on to the incidents themselves and I wouldn't want to interrupt that. But whatever you wish. We can do it tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given that the Chamber has another hearing at quarter past 2.00, the Chamber will rise for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 29th day of May, 2013, at 9.00 a.m.
